Neonatal body mass in the Single-striped grass mouse (Lemniscomys rosalia) is quite modest, with newborns typically weighing approximately 2.6 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.6 grams]. This initial mass is low compared to other murid rodents of similar ultimate adult size. When maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a body temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], the period of gestation extends for approximately 24 days [tg = approximately 24 days], a duration that is consistent with the general pattern observed in related striped grass mice. This relatively short gestation is followed by a rapid phase of neonatal development, during which the altricial pups are entirely dependent on maternal care and milk. The transition to nutritional independence occurs early in the life cycle of this species.

Weaning, marking the cessation of lactation and the onset of solid food consumption, occurs at 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. This early weaning age reflects a strategy common among small-bodied murids, where rapid offspring development is favored to reduce the duration of high maternal energetic investment. The pups transition quickly from a milk-based diet to seeds and invertebrates, which dominate the adult diet. Following weaning, the young enter a pre-reproductive juvenile phase during which they must attain a sufficient body size and physiological maturity before they can breed. The next major developmental milestone after nutritional independence is the onset of sexual maturation, a critical step that determines the species' generation time and population turnover rate. Field studies on related taxa provide comparative data for this species.

Female Single-striped grass mice attain puberty relatively late for a rodent of their stature, at 148 days since birth [tp = 148 days since birth] under standard captive conditions at 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. This value, based on observations of the congener Lemniscomys striatus, suggests a somewhat delayed reproductive maturation, which may be linked to ecological factors such as seasonal resource availability or predation pressure. The post-weaning juvenile phase thus lasts several months, allowing for substantial somatic growth before the first ovulation event. Once sexually mature, these rodents are capable of breeding throughout much of the year under favorable conditions. The adult body mass that females ultimately achieve is an important determinant of their reproductive output and competitive ability. This asymptotic size is shaped by both genetic and environmental factors.

The ultimate wet weight of adult individuals, based on data from the closely related Lemniscomys striatus, is approximately 42 grams [Wwi = approximately 42 grams]. This adult body mass places the Single-striped grass mouse in a moderate size range among African murid rodents. Data on lifespan, also inferred from the congener, indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 4.8 years [am = approximately 4.8 years] under ideal captive care maintained at 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. Such a lifespan is notably long for a rodent of this mass, suggesting a relatively slow pace of life compared to many similar-sized murids. This extended longevity may be linked to the species' social structure or its ability to buffer against environmental fluctuations. The combination of a delayed puberty and a long potential lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons across an individual's life.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a moderate litter size coupled with a high potential breeding frequency under optimal conditions. Females produce litters of approximately 4.2 pups [N_R_i = litters of approximately 4.2 pups] per parturition event. With the capacity to produce up to approximately 6 litters per year [F_R_i = up to approximately 6 litters per year], the annual reproductive rate is substantial. Work with captive colonies maintained at 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C] has demonstrated that this maximum reproductive rate is achievable when high-quality food and stable thermal conditions are provided. The combination of a moderate litter size with frequent breeding events allows for rapid population growth during favorable seasons, a life-history strategy that is well-suited to the disturbed grassland habitats this species occupies. The total lifetime reproductive success is thus influenced by both the number and the timing of litters a female can produce before reaching the end of her natural lifespan, which, as noted, may extend to nearly five years.
